questions.stem: Martha, 48, a laboratory scientist, tells you at her GP visit that she has felt "so awfully tired" for several months and it is getting worse. You want to work out early whether this is sleepiness or fatigue. Which question does this best?
options: "Do you feel weak or short of breath when you climb stairs?"
"How many hours of sleep do you usually get each night?"
"Do you nod off when you sit still, such as watching TV or reading?"
"Have you lost interest in the things you used to enjoy?"
questions.why: Sleepiness means dozing off when inactive, and it points to a sleep disorder such as OSA. Fatigue is a lack of energy without falling asleep. Patients use "tired" for both, so ask directly whether they nod off.
notes: This screens for anaemia or heart and lung disease, which cause fatigue or breathlessness. It does not tell you whether she actually falls asleep.
Hours of sleep are part of the sleep history, but Martha sleeps about 7 hours and still dozes, so the answer does not separate sleepiness from fatigue.
This screens for anhedonia in depression, which is one of the differentials. It does not tell you whether her tiredness means dozing off.

questions.stem: Martha, 48, comes back to the GP. ESS 15, STOP-Bang 5, OSA50 6, BMI 36, neck 42 cm. FBC, iron studies and TSH are normal. After long days she sometimes feels drowsy driving home. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm and grade the likely diagnosis?
options: Request an unattended home sleep study directly, marked urgent for drowsy driving
Start auto-titrating CPAP now and review her sleepiness score in four weeks
Arrange overnight pulse oximetry and refer only if desaturations are recorded
Refer to ENT for assessment for upper airway surgery before any sleep study
questions.why: Her scores meet the MBS criteria for a GP to request a home sleep study directly: ESS 8 or more plus STOP-Bang 4 or more or OSA50 5 or more. Polysomnography confirms OSA and grades it by AHI. Drowsy driving makes it urgent.
notes: CPAP is first line for moderate to severe OSA, but only once a sleep study has confirmed and graded it. Starting it on questionnaire scores alone is premature.
Oximetry alone cannot reliably diagnose or grade OSA, because it gives no AHI and misses hypopnoeas with arousals. A normal result would not rule OSA out.
Surgery is an alternative for selected patients after the diagnosis is confirmed and CPAP has failed. It is not how OSA is diagnosed.

questions.stem: Martha, 48, has probable obstructive sleep apnoea and drinks one or two glasses of wine before bed most nights "to help me sleep". You advise her to stop drinking in the evening. By what main mechanism does alcohol before bed make her OSA worse?
options: Bronchospasm narrows her lower airways while she is asleep
Brainstem respiratory drive stops, so she makes no effort to breathe
Nasal congestion forces her to breathe through her mouth
Pharyngeal dilator tone falls, so her narrow upper airway collapses
questions.why: During sleep the pharyngeal dilator muscles (mainly genioglossus) lose the drive they have when awake. Alcohol reduces their tone further and raises the arousal threshold, so her already crowded oropharynx collapses more often and for longer.
notes: OSA is a collapse of the upper airway (the pharynx), not narrowing of the lower airways. Bronchospasm is the mechanism in asthma.
Loss of respiratory drive with no effort to breathe is central sleep apnoea. In OSA she keeps trying to breathe against a closed airway.
Alcohol can congest the nose a little, but that is minor. The main effect is relaxation of the pharyngeal muscles and a higher threshold for waking.

questions.stem: Martha, 48, has a BMI of 36 and a crowded oropharynx. In OSA, the genioglossus loses tone during sleep, so the base of the tongue falls back against the posterior pharyngeal wall. Which nerve supplies this muscle?
options: Vagus nerve via the pharyngeal plexus (CN X)
Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3)
questions.why: The hypoglossal nerve supplies all the intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus, including genioglossus, the main airway dilator that pulls the tongue forward. Hypoglossal nerve stimulation is an option for selected patients who cannot tolerate CPAP.
notes: CN IX gives taste and general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue, and its only motor supply is stylopharyngeus. It does not supply genioglossus.
The pharyngeal plexus of CN X supplies the pharyngeal constrictors, most of the soft palate and palatoglossus, but not genioglossus.
CN V3 supplies the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric, plus general sensation to the anterior tongue. It does not supply the tongue muscles.
